client: I just don't see the point in doing normal things anymore since my brother died. Everything feels empty, and I've stopped reaching out to friends because they don't really understand what I'm going through. I'm not sure talking about it will help - the pain just feels permanent.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying such deep grief that even everyday activities feel meaningless now. I hear how isolating this pain feels when others don't fully understand. Would you be willing to share what comes up when you say the pain feels permanent?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: It just feels like this heavy weight that never lifts, you know? Even when I try to distract myself or go through the motions of daily life, the sadness is always there in the background. People tell me "time heals" but it's been months and I don't feel any better - that's what makes it seem permanent.
therapist: Your voice carries so much more pain than your words alone express—this grief sounds utterly exhausting to carry. When you talk about going through the motions, I wonder what happens when that sadness in the background comes forward—what does it need you to know right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know what it needs me to know—that's the problem. The sadness just feels like this heavy weight that makes everything harder, but when I try to focus on it, my mind just goes blank. Sometimes I think maybe it's trying to tell me I'm failing at life, but that just makes me feel worse.
therapist: That blank space when you try to focus on the sadness sounds both frustrating and frightening. I notice when you mention failing at life, your voice drops—could we slow down and explore where that thought comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know where that thought comes from exactly...it's just always there in the background. When I try to focus on it, I get this tight feeling in my chest like I'm about to drown in all my failures. 

It's easier to just keep busy than to actually sit with these feelings. When you ask me to slow down, part of me wants to run away from this conversation.
therapist: That tightness in your chest sounds like it's holding so much—both the urge to run and the fear of drowning in these feelings. Would it feel safer if we approached this slowly, like dipping a toe in the water rather than diving in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but dipping a toe feels like I’m not really doing anything about it. I just keep feeling this pressure, like I need to fix it now or it’ll get worse. Sometimes I worry that if I don’t dive in, I’ll never get past this anxiety.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between the pressure to act quickly and the fear of what might happen if you don't—that's an incredibly difficult space to be in. What would it feel like to approach this with curiosity rather than urgency?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know if curiosity is really possible right now. When I try to slow down and be curious, my brain just floods with all the worst-case scenarios. It feels like if I don't make a decision immediately, I'll miss some critical window and everything will fall apart.
therapist: It sounds like trying to be curious feels almost impossible when those worst-case scenarios rush in. When you talk about missing a critical window, I wonder if we could explore what that window represents for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess that window represents a sense of urgency, like if I don’t act perfectly or quickly enough, everything will fall apart. It’s hard to even think about exploring it because it feels so real and immediate when I’m in that anxious spiral. Honestly, trying to unpack it feels overwhelming—like I’m just going to make it worse by focusing on it.
therapist: That sense of urgency feels so real and immediate when you're in that spiral—it sounds exhausting to carry. When you say unpacking it feels overwhelming, could we try approaching it in smaller, more manageable pieces?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about breaking it down, but even small pieces feel like too much right now. When I try to focus on just one part of my anxiety, my brain immediately jumps to all the other things I should be worrying about. It's like trying to hold water in my hands - the more I try to contain it, the more it spills everywhere.
therapist: That image of trying to hold water in your hands—it really captures how slippery and overwhelming these thoughts feel when you try to focus on them. What happens if, instead of trying to contain them, we just notice them flowing by?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I see what you're saying, but it feels like those thoughts aren't just flowing by—they're crashing into me like waves. When I try to notice them without holding on, I just end up feeling even more out of control. It’s like I’m drowning in them instead of letting them pass.
therapist: Those waves sound absolutely exhausting—like no matter how you try to approach them, they keep knocking you down. When you say you feel like you're drowning in them, where in your body do you notice that sensation most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
It's mostly in my chest—this tight, heavy feeling like I can't take a full breath. And my stomach gets all twisted up too. It's worse at night when I'm alone with my thoughts, just waiting for the next wave of anxiety to hit. 

I've tried deep breathing before, but it never seems to help much in the moment. My mind just races faster when I try to focus on it.
therapist: That tightness in your chest and twisted stomach sound so physically overwhelming, especially at night when everything feels quieter and those thoughts seem louder. When you say deep breathing doesn't help because your mind races faster, what happens if we try something simpler—like just noticing the sensation of your breath, without trying to change it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
